analysis.one_liner: Phases out and repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax.
analysis.headline: The estate-tax repeal bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from January 1999 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would gradually raise the amount of an inheritance exempt from federal estate tax to $5 million by 2004, then repeal the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax entirely starting in 2005 [S2][S3]. Only large estates ever pay these taxes, so the benefit would flow to the wealthiest families. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of large estates. The tax applies only to estates above the exclusion amount, which the bill would raise from $1 million in 2000 to $5 million by 2004 before repeal in 2005 — and it would apply that bigger exclusion retroactively to deaths after the end of 1997 [S3]. The sponsor argued repeal would also help family farms and encourage savings, citing findings that farmers are more likely to face the tax [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the per-person estate-tax exclusion from $1 million in 2000 to $5 million by 2004, so estates below those levels owe nothing, and applies the increases retroactively to deaths after December 31, 1997 [S3].
Fully repeals the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax for deaths and transfers after December 31, 2004, eliminating the tax on the largest inheritances entirely [S2][S3].
The bill's findings argue repeal would aid family-farm preservation, noting that most farms and ranches are family-owned and that farmers are said to be more likely to owe estate taxes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury — and ultimately other taxpayers or government programs. The estate tax is paid only on the largest estates, so repealing it removes revenue that would otherwise come from the wealthiest families, meaning the same federal spending must be funded from other sources [S3].

drawbacks.text: The repeal eliminates a tax paid only by the largest estates, so its dollars flow overwhelmingly to the wealthiest families; since 1999 federal budget rules required tax cuts to be offset or fit within caps, the cost would have come out of other taxpayers or federal programs [S2][S3].
The retroactive provision (larger exclusions for deaths after the end of 1997) would refund tax already owed on estates settled before the bill could even pass [S3].

Repeal removes the estate tax as a backstop to the capital gains loophole: inherited assets get a stepped-up basis, so untaxed gains are never taxed at all once the estate tax is gone — a structural benefit limited to households with large appreciated holdings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are real but narrowly aimed: families with estates between $1 million and $5 million would gain the most during the phase-out, and full repeal mainly benefits heirs of very large fortunes. The cost is a permanent loss of federal revenue collected from the wealthiest households, which would be made up by other taxpayers or by cutting spending. The family-farm rationale in the findings is weakened by the structure of the tax itself — the exclusion increases protect virtually all farms well before full repeal — so the bill is best understood as a large tax cut concentrated at the top, not a broad relief measure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled any action on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Lugar introduced the bill on January 19, 1999, with five Republican cosponsors [S4][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, through the end of the 106th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate tax stayed in place, meaning the federal treasury continued collecting it from the largest estates, and other taxpayers did not have to make up the lost revenue. Heirs of very large estates lost the chance at the repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury and taxpayers who didn't inherit millions

for.name: Sen. Richard Lugar
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Chuck Hagel, Pat Roberts, and Jesse Helms, plus two additional Republican senators

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no recorded action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting it die.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democratic support appears in the record; the bill never advanced far enough for a roll-call vote [S4].

industries.note: The estate tax falls only on estates above the exclusion, so repeal is a direct transfer to the families with the largest fortunes. The bill would even apply its larger exclusions retroactively to deaths after 1997 [S3].

The bill's findings emphasize that farm and small-business estates can face the tax because their wealth is tied up in land and equipment; the rising exclusions would shield nearly all of them well before repeal [S3].

industries.industry: Estate planning, trust, and life insurance professionals
industries.note: Repealing the estate and gift taxes would eliminate a major market for estate-tax planning services and survivorship insurance products.
